result:
Solution 3 is the only one with a correct final answer, f(r,2) = 1/(2r). I checked it with a lower-bound argument and an explicit construction.

**Lower bound.** In each tree, a centroid-type edge cut gives a part of size between n/r and n/2. Take such a cut in each tree, with part sizes s₁ and s₂ (both at least n/r). Let a = |S₁∩S₂|. Then the cell |S₁∖S₂| equals s₁−a and the cell |S₂∖S₁| equals s₂−a. The cell outside both parts is large, because s₁ and s₂ are at most n/2. Take s₁ = s₂ = n/r as an illustration. The adversary can choose either the pair (a, outside cell) or the pair (s₁−a, s₂−a). The first has minimum a and the second has minimum n/r−a. One of them is at least n/(2r). So f(r,2) ≥ 1/(2r).

**Upper bound.** Build the two trees so that the labels are independent (a product structure) across them.
- Tree 1 has a root with r branches of size n/r each.
- Tree 2 has a root of degree 2 with halves of size n/2, each half splitting into r−1 branches.
- With independence, a cut pair with smaller-side fractions x and y is worth min(x,y)·(1−max(x,y)).
- The two best cut pairs give (1/r)(1/2) = 1/(2r) and (1/(2(r−1)))·((r−1)/r) = 1/(2r). Deeper cuts give less.

For r = 3 the best value is 1/6, which is below both 2/9 (Solution 1) and 1/5 (Solution 2). That rules out Solutions 1 and 2, since f(3,2) ≤ 1/6. At r = 2 all three formulas give 1/4, so that case cannot separate them.

I did not independently prove the matching upper bound for every r, so the claim that 1/(2r) is exact for all r rests on the construction above and the lower bound.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: ACCEPT
